blk_part_01_what_makes_a_wine_fortified.text: The second thing the spirit does depends on when it goes in. Yeast cannot live in such strong alcohol. Picture two barrels of the same grape juice. In the first, makers pour in spirit while fermentation is still going on. The yeast stops, a lot of sugar is left, and the wine stays sweet. This is how port is made. In the second barrel, makers wait until fermentation is over and the sugar is gone. The wine is dry. This is how dry sherry, such as fino, is made. For them, the spirit has a different job: it decides how the wine ages, as you will see later.

blk_part_02_fortified_wine_and_the_sea_t.text: Sherry was the first star. It comes from the area around Jerez, a city in southern Spain. The word sherry is simply the English way of saying Jerez. In 1587 the English sailor Francis Drake attacked Cádiz, a city by the sea not far from Jerez. He carried home about 2,900 barrels of sherry. People in England loved it and called it sack, and it soon became a favourite drink there.

blk_part_02_fortified_wine_and_the_sea_t.text: Port came out of a war. In the late 1600s, England and France were enemies, so England stopped buying wine from France. Merchants from England turned to Portugal instead. In 1703 the two countries signed the Methuen Treaty, an agreement about trade. Because of it, wine from Portugal paid much less tax than wine from France. Red wine from the Douro valley in northern Portugal had a long way to go by sea. So the merchants added spirit to keep it safe on the trip. British merchants built this trade. That is why many port houses, the companies that make port, still have British names, such as Taylor's and Graham's.

blk_part_02_fortified_wine_and_the_sea_t.text: Madeira is an island of Portugal in the Atlantic Ocean. Ships going to America and Asia often stopped there. Merchants from England lived on the island and ran most of its wine trade. They put barrels of wine on the ships, with spirit added so it would survive. Then something surprising happened. The heat in the hold, the space at the bottom of the ship, made the wine taste better. Wine that travelled the full round trip was called vinho da roda, or wine of the round trip. It became very popular.

blk_part_03_port_sherry_and_madeira_toda.text: For port, it is the place where it ages. Port grows old in big buildings called lodges. Many of them are in Vila Nova de Gaia, the town across the Douro river from Porto. These lodges stand on the south bank of the river, so they face north, away from the sun. The air inside stays cool and damp, and the wine ages slowly. Some port houses, such as Taylor's, now also have modern lodges in the Douro valley. They keep the same cool, damp air. Visitors who tour a lodge usually try two styles. Ruby port ages only a short time, so it stays bright red and tastes of fresh fruit. Tawny port ages for years in wooden barrels. A little air comes in through the wood, so the wine slowly turns golden brown and tastes of nuts.

blk_part_03_port_sherry_and_madeira_toda.text: For sherry, it is flor, a layer of yeast on top of the wine. It covers the wine in the barrel like a thin white blanket. The flor keeps the air away, so fino and manzanilla stay pale, dry and fresh. But flor can only live if the alcohol is not too strong. So for these wines, makers add only a little spirit, to about 15 percent alcohol. For oloroso, they add more, to about 17 percent. No flor can grow, and air slowly turns the wine dark and rich. A small difference in spirit makes two very different wines.

blk_part_05_how_people_drink_fortified_w.text: In the Charente, Pineau is an aperitif, a drink before the meal. Its fresh grape taste is best when it is cold, so people serve it at about 8 to 10 degrees. They do not add ice, because the ice would melt and make the drink weaker. A summer favourite is melon au Pineau. You cut a small Charentais melon in half, take out the seeds and pour Pineau into the middle. The two belong together. The melon is named after the same region, and its sweet fruit matches the sweet grape taste of the drink.

The bottle is passed to the left, so it goes around the table in one direction and reaches everyone. If someone keeps it too long, a guest may ask: Do you know the Bishop of Norwich? A bishop is a church leader, and Norwich is a city in England. One Bishop of Norwich often fell asleep at dinner, so the port stopped next to him. The question is a polite way to say: please pass the bottle.
